a: Ignatius, also called Theophorus
p: Ignatius gives himself a second name at the head of every letter: Theophorus, 'God-bearer'.
b: Greek Ignatios ho kai Theophoros, 'Ignatius, who is also Theophorus'. The second name means 'God-bearer' (theos, 'God', and pherō, 'carry'). Lake's footnote gives the story told in the third-century Acts of Ignatius: the emperor asks, 'And who is Theophorus?' and Ignatius answers, 'He who has Christ in his heart.' The Orthodox Church in America's life of the saint gives two reasons for the name: he 'bore God in his heart', and, by tradition, he was the child Christ held in his arms. He gives himself no title in this greeting; his one title in this letter comes at 2:2.
orig: Ἰγνάτιος, ὁ καὶ Θεοφόρος (Ignatios, ho kai Theophoros)

a: presides in the region of the Romans
p: The Greek verb means 'sit in the front seat'. Where and over what the Roman church presides is debated.
b:
Greek prokathētai, 'sits first, presides', from pro, 'in front', and kathēmai, 'sit'. Lightfoot shows the word used of a leading city that 'presides' over a region (Antioch 'presides over the East' in an edict quoted by John Malalas). Lake: 'which also has the presidency in the country of the land of the Romans'.

Lightfoot weighs two readings of 'in the region of the Romans'. (1) They give 'the limits over which the supremacy or jurisdiction extends': Rome's is 'the principal church in this region'. (2) They give 'the locality of the supreme power itself', a precedence 'over the other churches of Christendom', akin to the 'potentior principalitas' Irenaeus gives Rome (Against Heresies 3.3.2). He takes the first and concludes: 'The idea of the "cathedra Petri" therefore has no place here.' More in chapter 1; the readings of the churches are in the note on 'presiding over the love'.
orig: ἥτις καὶ προκάθηται ἐν τόπῳ χωρίου Ῥωμαίων (hētis kai prokathētai en topō chōriou Rhōmaiōn)

a: presiding over the love
t: 'Presiding over the love': how it is read
p: 'The love' may mean love itself or the whole fellowship of churches. Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican voices read the greeting differently.
b:
Greek prokathēmenē tēs agapēs; Lake: 'pre-eminent in love'. 'The love' (agapē) is read in two senses: (1) charity, love itself; (2) a name for the whole fellowship of churches, as Ignatius can call a body of believers 'the love' (9:3).

Catholic: Vatican II speaks of 'the primacy of the Chair of Peter, which presides over the whole assembly of charity', citing this greeting (Lumen Gentium 13, note 11), so sense 2; the Catechism, of 'the Church of Rome "which presides in charity"' (Catechism 834).

Orthodox: the theologian Thomas Hopko: the Roman church 'held this place of honor and exercised a "presidency in love"', because Peter and Paul founded it and it was the church of the capital (sense 1).

Lightfoot, Anglican scholar and Bishop of Durham: 'The Church of Rome, as it is first in rank, is first also in love' (sense 1); 'The idea of the "cathedra Petri" therefore has no place here.'

Peter's successors: the card at Matthew 16:18.

a: worthy of God
p: Ignatius strings six compound words that all begin with 'worthy'.
b: Each is one Greek word built on axios, 'worthy': axiotheos 'worthy of God', axioprepēs 'worthy of honor', axiomakaristos 'worthy to be called blessed', axiepainos 'worthy of praise', axiepiteuktos 'worthy to reach its goal' (from the same verb as 'reach God', see the note at 1:2), and axiagnos 'worthy in purity'. His praise of their faces, 'worthy of God', in 1:1 uses the same family, and Lightfoot notes how often Ignatius uses compounds of axios. The Plain English Translation keeps all six.
orig: ἀξιόθεος, ἀξιοπρεπής, ἀξιομακάριστος, ἀξιέπαινος, ἀξιεπίτευκτος, ἀξίαγνος

a: Jesus Christ our God
p: Ignatius calls Jesus 'our God' twice in this greeting, without any softening.
b: Greek Iēsou Christou tou theou hēmōn, 'of Jesus Christ the God of us'. The phrase comes twice in this greeting and again at 3:3 ('our God, Jesus Christ'), and at 6:3 Ignatius speaks of 'the suffering of my God'. The Plain English Translation renders it exactly. Ignatius also keeps the Son distinct from the Father: Jesus is 'his only Son' and 'the Father's Son' in this same greeting. The New Testament has the same boldness in a few places (John 1:1; John 20:28; Titus 2:13). How the churches came to state the Son's divinity is on the topic page.
orig: Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν (Iēsou Christou, tou theou hēmōn)

a: filtered clean of every foreign stain
p: The verb is a wine-maker's word: strained through a filter until no other color is left.
b: Greek apodiylismenois, from diylizō, 'strain through a filter', the verb of Matthew 23:24, 'filtering out the gnat'. Lake renders 'filtered clear from every foreign stain'. The 'color' (chrōma) is a stain that does not belong. Ignatius praises the Roman church as free of false teaching, the danger his other letters fight; he warns the Romans of nothing of that kind. Contrast the letters to Ephesus and Smyrna, where he must warn against teachers who deny Christ's flesh.
orig: ἀποδιϋλισμένοις ἀπὸ παντὸς ἀλλοτρίου χρώματος (apodiylismenois apo pantos allotriou chrōmatos)

a: I am in chains
p: Ignatius writes from Smyrna, under guard, to the city where he is going to die.
b: Greek dedemenos, 'bound'. Eusebius writes that 'the story is' (logos d' echei) that Ignatius was sent from Syria to the city of the Romans and became food for wild beasts because of his witness to Christ, and that he made the journey through Asia 'under the closest watch of guards' (Church History 3.36.3-4). The letter is dated at Smyrna (10:1, 3), before he reached Rome. Lake says that every letter but this one was written to thank a church; this one 'has the object of preventing the Christians at Rome from making any efforts to save Ignatius from the beasts in the arena, and so robbing him of the crown of martyrdom'.
orig: δεδεμένος γὰρ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ (dedemenos gar en Christō Iēsou)

a: reach God
p: One verb runs through the letter: to reach, gain or arrive at God.
b: Greek tou theou epitychein. The verb epitynchanō means to hit the mark, gain what one aims at. Ignatius uses it again and again for his death: 'reach God' (1:2; 2:1; 4:1; 9:2), 'reach Jesus Christ' (5:3, twice), and with no object at all at 8:3 (Lake: 'Pray for me that I may attain'), where the Plain English Translation supplies 'God'. Lake renders 'attain to God'. The same verb is behind 'obtain the grace' earlier in this verse and 'he has granted' in 1:1 (Lightfoot: 'I have been successful', 'it has been granted me'), so the whole letter turns on getting what one prays for. The Plain English Translation uses 'reach' every time the goal is God or Christ.

a: Your love frightens me
p: Ignatius fears that Roman Christians with influence will get him released.
b: Lake: the letter's object is 'preventing the Christians at Rome from making any efforts to save Ignatius from the beasts'. The letter shows they could: 'it is easy for you to do what you want' (1:2); 'if you keep silent' (2:1); 'do not become an untimely kindness to me' (4:1). It does not say how. Lightfoot explains 'if you do not spare me' as 'should interpose to rob me of my desire': to Ignatius, death in the arena is life (6:2, 'Do not keep me from living'), so whoever saves his body wrongs him.

a: my lot
p: Greek kleros, 'lot' or 'share': the portion God has assigned him.
b: Greek klēros, the lot cast to divide land, then a share or inheritance. Ignatius means the death God has given him to die. The same word gave English 'clergy', but that sense is later.

a: I do not want you to please people
p: Ignatius borrows Paul's contrast between pleasing people and pleasing God.
b: Greek anthrōpareskēsai ... theō aresai. Lake's margin points to 1 Thessalonians 2:4: 'We do not aim to please people. We aim to please God' (1 Thessalonians 2:4). Paul says it of himself; Ignatius turns it on the Romans. To 'please people' here would be to do the kind thing that keeps him alive; to please God is to let him go.
orig: Οὐ γὰρ θέλω ὑμᾶς ἀνθρωπαρεσκῆσαι, ἀλλὰ θεῷ ἀρέσαι

a: I am a word of God
t: A word, or only a sound
p: If he dies, his life speaks for God; if he is saved, he is noise that means nothing.
b: Greek egō logos theou ... palin esomai phōnē. Logos is a word with meaning; phōnē is a voice or a sound, which may be only noise. The first clause has no verb ('I, a word of God'); Lake: 'I am a word of God; but if you love my flesh, I shall again be only a cry.' Lightfoot defends the short form: 'the terse and characteristic ἐγὼ λόγος Θεοῦ is correct', against editors who added 'I will become'. He reports that John the Monk, in the later 300s, explained the passage by the Word and the Voice of John 1:1, 14 and 23 (the Baptist, 'a voice'), and he accepts that sense: 'His martyrdom alone would make his life an intelligible utterance; otherwise it was no better than the passionate cry of some irrational creature.' Some witnesses read 'running' for 'sound' (see the variant). The verb for 'fall in love' (erasthēte) is the verb of erōs, desire, which comes back at 7:2.
orig: ἐγὼ λόγος θεοῦ· ἐὰν δὲ ἐρασθῆτε τῆς σαρκός μου, πάλιν ἔσομαι φωνή

a: poured out to God as a drink offering
p: Ignatius pictures his death as wine poured on an altar, as Paul did his own.
b: Greek spondisthēnai theō, 'be poured out as a libation to God'. The verb, spondizō, is from the same family as Paul's spendomai, which he uses of his own coming death: 'even if I am being poured out as a drink offering' (Philippians 2:17) and 'For I am already a drink offering being poured out' (2 Timothy 4:6). Lightfoot: 'The idea is taken from S. Paul'. The 'altar' that is 'still ready' carries on the picture: the arena is the place of sacrifice. Lake notes that the 'choir' of the next sentence is 'probably from the chorus or choir which gathered round the altar in heathen ceremonial, and sang a sacrificial hymn'.
orig: τοῦ σπονδισθῆναι θεῷ, ὡς ἔτι θυσιαστήριον ἕτοιμόν ἐστιν

a: the overseer of Syria
p: Ignatius's one title for himself in this letter is here: overseer, the word behind 'bishop'.
b: Greek ton episkopon Syrias. Episkopos, 'overseer', is the word behind 'bishop'; the Plain English Translation says 'overseer' as in its New Testament (Philippians 1:1). Ignatius names himself by the province, not the city: Antioch was the capital of the Roman province of Syria. Eusebius says he was the second in the succession from Peter at Antioch to receive the office of overseer (Church History 3.36.2), and Jerome calls him 'third bishop of the church of Antioch after Peter the apostle' (Lives of Illustrious Men 16). Lake's note: 'According to tradition Peter was the first and Euodius the second'.

a: at the sunset, after sending for him from the sunrise
p: The words for west and east are 'setting' and 'rising': Ignatius will set like the sun and rise again.
b: Greek eis dysin apo anatolēs: dysis, the sun's setting, is the west; anatolē, its rising, is the east. Then: 'It is good to set (dynai) ... so that I may rise (anateilō) to him.' Rome is in the west; his death there is a sunset that leads to a sunrise. 1 Clement, sent from Rome, says that Paul 'came to the far limit of the West' (1 Clement 5:7). Lightfoot points out how Ignatius mixes the picture with the thing it pictures, as again at 4:3.
orig: εἰς δύσιν ἀπὸ ἀνατολῆς ... καλὸν τὸ δῦναι ... ἵνα εἰς αὐτὸν ἀνατείλω

a: You have never envied anyone; you taught others
p: Ignatius praises the Roman church as a teacher of other churches.
b: He may be thinking of letters such as 1 Clement, sent by 'the church of God that lives as a resident alien in Rome' to the church at Corinth (1 Clement 1:0). Lightfoot points to Dionysius of Corinth, writing to Rome about AD 170, who praises the Romans' custom 'from the beginning' of doing good to all the brothers in many ways and sending supplies to many churches in every city (Eusebius, Church History 4.23). Ignatius's point: you have taught others to stand firm; now let what you teach hold good for him as well.

a: be called a Christian but also be found one
p: Ignatius uses the word 'Christian', and he makes the name something to live up to.
b: Greek Christianos. The New Testament uses the word three times (Acts 11:26, at Ignatius's own city of Antioch; Acts 26:28; 1 Peter 4:16), and 1 Peter already ties it to suffering: 'But if it is for being a Christian, there is no shame in it' (1 Peter 4:16). Lightfoot paraphrases Ignatius: 'If I am proved a Christian by my martyrdom, then I shall certainly be recognised as' one. 'Found' (heurethō) is a word Ignatius keeps using for the day of trial: 'found pure bread' (4:1), 'found a sacrifice' (4:2).
orig: ἵνα μὴ μόνον λέγωμαι Χριστιανὸς ἀλλὰ καὶ εὑρεθῶ

a: inside and out
p: Strength of will and strength of body.
b: Greek esōthen te kai exōthen. Lightfoot: 'with moral courage and with physical endurance', close to Ignatius's frequent pair 'flesh and spirit'.

a: is seen all the more
p: Nothing seen is good; Christ, now unseen with the Father, is seen more than ever.
b: Greek mallon phainetai, 'appears more'. Lake's footnote: 'The sentence is clumsily expressed: apparently Ignatius means "nothing directly visible is good, and Jesus Christ, who is no longer visible, being in the Father, is more clearly perceived by the eye of faith," but he has sacrificed clearness to a paradoxical playing with the words.' The thought is close to Paul: 'What we see lasts only a while; what we cannot see lasts forever' (2 Corinthians 4:18). Ignatius applies it to himself too: he will be truly faithful 'when the world no longer sees me' (3:2), and truly a disciple 'when the world does not even see my body' (4:2).

a: Christianity
p: Greek Christianismos, the faith as a whole. The New Testament never uses the word.
b: Greek Christianismos, formed like Ioudaismos, 'Judaism' (Galatians 1:13). The New Testament has 'Christian' but never 'Christianity'. Ignatius uses it here, in his letter To the Magnesians (chapter 10), where he sets it beside 'Judaism', and in To the Philadelphians (chapter 6). 'Not a work of persuading (peismonē) but of greatness': the faith is proved not by clever talk but by what it endures when the world hates it, the point of John 15:19: 'that is why the world hates you'. Lake: 'Christianity is not the work of persuasiveness, but of greatness, when it is hated by the world.'

a: I am dying for God willingly
t: Seeking death: how it has been judged
p: Ignatius begs not to be rescued. The Martyrdom of Polycarp, a generation later, warns against those who give themselves up.
b:
Ignatius has been arrested and condemned; he does not provoke the arrest, but he asks the Romans not to save him and says he will 'force' the beasts if they hold back (5:2). Eusebius tells of the letter's plea that the Romans not deprive him of his hope by begging him off from martyrdom, and quotes chapter 5 (Church History 3.36.6-9). The Martyrdom of Polycarp, from Smyrna a generation later, tells of Quintus, who 'pushed himself and some others to come forward of their own accord' and then gave way, and says 'we give no praise to people who turn themselves in, because that is not what the gospel teaches' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 4:1).

The two are not the same case: Ignatius was already condemned, while Quintus came forward of his own accord. Paul too wanted 'to leave and be with Christ' (Philippians 1:23) and still chose to stay for the churches' sake (Philippians 1:24-25).
r: Philippians 1:21-24; Acts 21:13; Martyrdom of Polycarp 4:1; Revelation 2:10

a: an untimely kindness
p: Ignatius quotes part of a Greek saying: an untimely kindness is no better than hatred.
b: Greek eunoia akairos. Lake's footnote: 'Apparently a partial quotation from the proverb preserved by Zenobius', akairos eunoi' ouden echthras diapherei, 'an unseasonable kindness is nothing different from hostility'. The Romans' well-meant rescue would be, in effect, an enemy's act.

a: I am God's wheat
p: Ignatius pictures himself as grain ground into flour, to be baked as pure bread.
b:
Greek sitos eimi theou. Wheat is ground in a mill; the beasts' teeth are the millstones; the flour becomes 'pure bread'. Lightfoot: 'He was the grain of God; by the teeth of the wild beasts he would be ground into fine flour; thus he would become a pure sacrificial loaf fit for the altar of God.' Compare 'God's bread, which is the flesh of Jesus Christ' (7:3) and Paul's 'there is one loaf, we who are many are one body' (1 Corinthians 10:17). Jesus too spoke of the grain of wheat that must fall and die to bear fruit (John 12:24).

Irenaeus, about 180, quotes the line without naming Ignatius. In his Greek, which Eusebius preserves, he introduces it 'as one of ours said, condemned to the beasts because of his witness toward God', and the words end simply 'pure bread' (Church History 3.36.12; Against Heresies 5.28.4). The Latin translation of Irenaeus, as Lightfoot reports it, has 'wheat of Christ' and 'bread of God'. Jerome's Latin puts the saying in Ignatius's mouth when he heard the lions roaring: Frumentum Christi sum, dentibus bestiarum molar, ut panis mundus inveniar, 'I am Christ's wheat; let me be ground by the teeth of beasts, so that I may be found pure bread' (Lives of Illustrious Men 16). See the variant on 'of Christ'.
orig: σῖτός εἰμι θεοῦ καὶ δι᾽ ὀδόντων θηρίων ἀλήθομαι

a: Coax the wild beasts
p: The verb is 'flatter, wheedle': Ignatius asks them to coax the animals, not to hold them back.
b: Greek kolakeusate, 'flatter, fawn on'. He uses the same verb of himself at 5:2: 'I will even coax them to eat me up quickly.' Lake: 'entice'. The joke is grim on purpose: the Romans want to persuade the authorities; Ignatius tells them to persuade the animals.

a: I will not be a burden to anyone
p: If nothing is left of him, no one will have to bury him.
b: Lightfoot takes the words as referring to 'the difficulties of sepulture in a strange city and at a season of trouble'. Later tradition did tell of remains: Jerome says 'the remains of his body lie in Antioch outside the Daphnitic gate in the cemetery' (Lives of Illustrious Men 16), and the Orthodox Church in America's life says the lions left 'only his heart and a few bones'.

a: through these tools
p: His death as an offering to God, the picture of 2:2 again.
b: Greek thysia, 'sacrifice'. Some witnesses read 'a sacrifice to God' or 'of God' (see the variant on 'a sacrifice'). The 'tools' (organa) are the beasts; Lightfoot: 'these instruments of my purification'. Paul asks the Romans to place their bodies before God 'as a sacrifice that is alive' (Romans 12:1); Ignatius, writing to the same church, asks to be made a dead one.
orig: διὰ τῶν ὀργάνων τούτων θυσία εὑρεθῶ

a: as Peter and Paul did
t: What 4:3 shows about Peter in Rome
p: Ignatius links Peter and Paul with the Roman church; he does not say what Peter did there.
b:
Ignatius's verb is his own, diatassomai, 'I command'; what the apostles did is left unsaid. Lightfoot fills it in: they 'are especially mentioned, because they had been at Rome and had given commandments (dietaxanto, his supplied verb) to the Roman Church', and he notes that the two names are joined in 'the earliest document emanating from, as well as in the earliest document addressed to, the Roman Church' after their deaths: 1 Clement 5:4-7 and this letter. 1 Clement says Peter 'bore his witness' and Paul 'came to the far limit of the West' (1 Clement 5:4; 1 Clement 5:7).

What the verse does not say: it does not name a bishop of Rome, speak of Peter's death in the city, or give Peter a role apart from Paul. Ignatius's point is humility: they were apostles and free; he is a condemned man and a slave. On the wider questions see the Peter topic and the card at Matthew 16:18.

a: I am a condemned man
p: Greek katakritos: one sentenced by a court.
b: Greek katakritos, 'condemned', a convict under sentence. Lightfoot: 'They visited you, as Apostles, as accredited delegates of God: I only as a convict.' He compares Paul's 'Am I not free? Am I not an apostle?' (1 Corinthians 9:1), where the same two words stand side by side.

a: Jesus Christ's freed person
p: A slave set free was a freedman of his former master. Ignatius will be Christ's.
b: Greek apeleutheros, a freed slave, who in Roman law still owed duties to the master who freed him. Lake's margin gives 1 Corinthians 7:22: 'a slave who was called in the Lord is the Lord's freed person' (1 Corinthians 7:22). (The digital text's margin reads '7, 29'; the printed page reads '7, 22'.) Ignatius uses the word for death and resurrection: 'if I suffer, I will become Jesus Christ's freed person, and I will rise free in him'.

a: I am fighting wild beasts
p: He uses Paul's phrase from 1 Corinthians 15:32 for the soldiers who guard him.
b: Greek thēriomachō, 'I fight wild beasts', the verb of 'As a mere man I fought with wild beasts at Ephesus' (1 Corinthians 15:32). Ignatius uses the word for his guards before he meets the real animals in Rome. Eusebius quotes 5:1-3 as proof of the letter and introduces it as 'word for word' (kata lexin), but his Greek differs in small ways: it leaves out 'cuttings and tearings apart' in 5:3, for one (see the variant there) (Church History 3.36.7-9).

a: ten leopards, that is, a squad of soldiers
p: Ignatius gives his own explanation: the 'leopards' are his guard of ten soldiers.
b: Greek deka leopardois, ho estin stratiōtikon tagma. Lake's footnote: 'The first impression made by this passage is that "leopards" was the name of some regiment, and that the following words are an explanatory gloss; but there is no evidence for this use of "leopard."' Tagma 'is perhaps the equivalent of "manipulus" in the later sense of "ten men."' And: 'it is the first instance of the word "leopard" in Greek or Latin literature.'
orig: δέκα λεοπάρδοις, ὅ ἐστιν στρατιωτικὸν τάγμα

a: but I am not justified by that
p: Ignatius uses Paul's words from 1 Corinthians 4:4.
b: Greek all' ou para touto dedikaiōmai. Lake's margin gives 1 Corinthians 4:4, where Paul writes all' ouk en toutō dedikaiōmai: 'I am aware of nothing against myself, but I am not justified by that' (1 Corinthians 4:4). The preposition differs; the sense is the same, so the Plain English Translation uses the site's wording. Suffering wrong makes him more of a disciple, but suffering does not make him righteous before God.

a: the beasts lost their nerve and never touched them
p: Ignatius knows of condemned Christians whom the animals would not touch.
b: Greek deilainomena ouch hēpsanto, 'being timid, they did not touch'. Ignatius does not say who these prisoners were. Compare the Martyrdom of Polycarp, where the young Germanicus, in the arena, 'forced the beast to come at him and dragged it onto himself' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 3:1). On beast fights and the arena, see the topic page.

a: Now I am beginning to be a disciple
p: A bishop of many years says that only now, on the way to death, does he begin to be a disciple.
b: Greek nyn archomai mathētēs einai. For Ignatius a disciple (mathētēs) is one who follows Christ all the way, to the cross; he will 'truly be a disciple' when the world no longer sees his body (4:2). Jesus's call stands behind it: 'Anyone who does not carry his own cross and come behind me cannot be a disciple of mine' (Luke 14:27). Eusebius's Greek of this verse has the same words, and Jerome's Latin reads Nunc incipio Christi esse discipulus, 'Now I begin to be Christ's disciple' (Church History 3.36.9; Lives of Illustrious Men 16).
orig: νῦν ἄρχομαι μαθητὴς εἶναι (nyn archomai mathētēs einai)

a: grinding of my whole body
p: The same root as 'ground' in 4:1: the mill picture returns in the list of tortures.
b: Greek alesmoi holou tou sōmatos, 'grindings of the whole body', from aleō, 'grind', the verb of 'I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts' (4:1). The long list (fire, cross, beasts, cutting, tearing, scattering of bones) names the deaths of the arena and the tortures used on condemned prisoners.

a: will do me no good
t: What good is the whole world?
p: Ignatius's 'profit' is the verb of Jesus's question about winning the whole world.
b: Greek ouden moi ōphelēsei, 'will profit me nothing'. Jesus asks with the same verb: 'What good will it do a person to win the whole world and pay for it with his life?' (Matthew 16:26). Lake's margin does not give it, and Ignatius's words are not a quotation; the Roberts and Donaldson English adds the saying itself after this sentence. 'The kingdoms of this age' recall the kingdoms the devil showed Jesus (Matthew 4:8).

a: It is better for me to die
p: Lake's margin compares Paul: 'I would rather die than have anyone make my boast empty.'
b: Greek kalon moi apothanein. Lake's margin gives 1 Corinthians 9:15, where Paul writes kalon gar moi mallon apothanein: 'I would rather die than have anyone make my boast empty' (1 Corinthians 9:15). 'To die into Christ Jesus' is literal (Greek eis, 'into'); Lake renders 'die in Christ Jesus'. Death is the way into Christ.
orig: καλόν μοι ἀποθανεῖν εἰς Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν

a: My birth is upon me
p: Ignatius calls his coming death his birth.
b: Greek ho de toketos moi epikeitai, 'the birth lies upon me': the labor pains have begun. Lake: 'The pains of birth are upon me.' A generation later the church at Smyrna kept the day of Polycarp's death as a birthday (the Martyrdom of Polycarp 18:3 speaks of gathering to 'celebrate the birthday of his martyrdom'). Here Ignatius says it first of himself: 'When I get there' (6:2), he will be born.

a: Do not keep me from living
p: Ignatius turns the words around: to save his body is to keep him from living.
b: Lightfoot: 'not θανεῖν, as we might have expected', 'die', but zēsai, 'live'. 'To Ignatius martyrdom is life.' So the next words are 'Do not want me to die', meaning do not keep him in this world. Jesus: 'anyone who loses his life because of me will find it' (Matthew 16:25).
orig: μὴ ἐμποδίσητέ μοι ζῆσαι (mē empodisēte moi zēsai)

a: I will become a human being
p: Ignatius says that only beyond death will he be fully a human being.
b: Greek anthrōpos esomai, 'I will be a human'. Lake: 'I shall become a man.' The thought: what God made a human being to be is reached only in God's presence, in 'pure light'. Ignatius calls Jesus Christ 'the new man' in his letter to the Ephesians (Ignatius to the Ephesians 20:1); compare Paul: 'We are to become a full-grown person' (Ephesians 4:13).

a: an imitator of the suffering of my God
p: Ignatius wants to imitate the Passion of Christ, whom he calls 'my God'.
b: Greek mimētēn einai tou pathous tou theou mou. Pathos, 'suffering', is the word behind 'the Passion'. 'Imitator' is Paul's word: 'Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ' (1 Corinthians 11:1). 'The suffering of my God' is one of Ignatius's boldest phrases: God suffered, in the flesh of Jesus. Later churches stated the point with care: the divine Son suffered in his human nature. Ignatius does not stop to explain; he wants to share it. See the note on 'Jesus Christ our God' in the greeting.
orig: μιμητὴν εἶναι τοῦ πάθους τοῦ θεοῦ μου

a: what holds me in its grip
p: The verb of 2 Corinthians 5:14, 'The love of Christ holds us in its grip'.
b: Greek ta synechonta me, 'the things that hold me fast'. Paul uses the verb: 'The love of Christ holds us in its grip' (2 Corinthians 5:14). Lake: 'the things which constrain me'.

a: The ruler of this age
p: Ignatius's name for the devil, built on Paul's 'rulers of this age'.
b: Greek ho archōn tou aiōnos toutou. Paul writes of 'the rulers of this age, who are coming to nothing' (1 Corinthians 2:6); John's Gospel calls him 'the world's ruler' (John 14:30). Ignatius uses the singular for Satan (also in his letter to the Ephesians), who 'wants to snatch me away', that is, to keep him from martyrdom by any means, kindness included. The friends who would rescue him would be helping the devil without knowing it.

a: My love has been crucified
p: The word is eros, desire. Lightfoot reads 'my earthly passion'; Origen read it of Christ.
b:
Greek ho emos erōs estaurōtai. Erōs is desire, the longing love of Greek poetry, not the New Testament's agapē. Lightfoot: erōs is found only twice in the Greek Old Testament, 'in both passages ... strong sensual passion', and never in the New Testament; so Ignatius 'would necessarily use ἔρως in a bad sense to denote the passions of his former unregenerate life. His ἀγάπη, we might say, was perfected, when his ἔρως was crucified.' He compares Galatians 5:24: 'Those who are Christ's have crucified the flesh, with its passions and its desires.'

Origen read it the other way: 'my Love', Christ, has been crucified. In the prologue to his Commentary on the Song of Songs, as Lightfoot quotes it, he says he remembers 'one of the saints, Ignatius by name', who said of Christ, 'My Love is crucified', and judged him not to blame. Lightfoot calls this 'a wholly different interpretation' and says later Greek writers followed Origen. The Orthodox Church in America's life renders the phrase 'In me, desire has been nailed to the cross'.
orig: ὁ ἐμὸς ἔρως ἐσταύρωται (ho emos erōs estaurōtai)

a: living water
p: Lake's margin points to John 4:10 and 7:38: the Spirit as living water inside the believer.
b: Greek hydōr zōn, 'living water', as in John 4:10: 'he would have given you living water'. John 7:38-39 says the 'rivers of living water' are the Spirit. In Ignatius the water speaks, and its word is 'Come to the Father', as Jesus said of his own death: 'I am on my way to the Father' (John 14:28). Lake: 'the text is much expanded in the later authorities', and Lightfoot was inclined to read 'leaping' with the long recension, as in John 4:14 (see the variant).
orig: ὕδωρ δὲ ζῶν καὶ λαλοῦν ἐν ἐμοί

a: no fire in me that loves material things
p: Greek philoülon, 'matter-loving': the fire of desire for the things of this world.
b: Greek pyr philoülon, from philos, 'loving', and hylē, 'matter, stuff'. The same hylē stood in 6:2: 'do not trick him with material things'. Fire that feeds on stuff has gone out; water that speaks of the Father has taken its place.

a: I want God's bread, which is the flesh of Jesus Christ
p: Ignatius's words sound like the Lord's Supper. Lightfoot, Zahn and Lake differ on how directly he means it.
b:
Greek arton theou thelō, ho estin sarx Iēsou Christou ... kai poma thelō to haima autou. 'God's bread' is the phrase of John 6:33, in Lake's margin; Jesus goes on, 'And the bread I will give is my flesh, for the sake of the world's life' (John 6:51). Elsewhere Ignatius says the thanksgiving 'is the flesh of our Savior' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 7:1).

Lightfoot: 'The reference here is not to the eucharist itself but to the union with Christ which is symbolized and pledged in the eucharist', the union Ignatius expects to complete through martyrdom; and 'it is impossible to be confident about the interpretation of language so obscure.' Zahn, as Lightfoot reports him, finds a secondary reference to the love-feast; Lightfoot thinks it 'barely possible'. Lake suggests a play on agapē as a name for the church's meal.

How the churches understand Christ's presence in the bread: the cards at Matthew 26:26 and John 6:53-58.

a: from David's seed
p: Lake's margin gives John 7:42, Romans 1:3 and 2 Timothy 2:8.
b: Greek tou ek spermatos Daueid. John 7:42 has the same words, ek tou spermatos Dauid: 'the Messiah comes from David's seed' (John 7:42). Paul says Jesus 'according to the flesh, came from the offspring of David' (Romans 1:3). Ignatius puts the phrase beside 'flesh' on purpose: Christ's real human descent is the ground of his real flesh, the point he presses against those who say his body only seemed real (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:1).
r: John 7:42; Romans 1:3; 2 Timothy 2:8; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:1

a: love that does not decay
p: Greek agape aphthartos: food that decays set against love that cannot.
b: Greek agapē aphthartos, 'love incorruptible'. The pair phthora / aphthartos, 'decay' / 'without decay', frames the verse: 'food that decays' at the start, 'love that does not decay' at the end. Lake's footnote suggests 'a play on the words', since agapē was also a name for a church meal (Jude 1:12, 'your love feasts').

a: so that you too may be wanted
p: Ignatius plays on one verb five times: want, will, be wanted.
b: Greek thelō ... thelēsēte ... thelēsate ... thelēthēte. 'Want it, so that you too may be wanted': if they will what he wills, God will will them, that is, accept them. Lake: 'Desire it, in order that you also may be desired.'

a: the mouth that does not lie
p: Jesus Christ is the Father's truthful mouth.
b: Greek to apseudes stoma. The adjective is the one of Titus 1:2, 'The God who does not lie'. Christ as the Father's mouth is close to John's 'Word' (John 1:1, 18): the Father speaks through him. Ignatius appeals to Christ to vouch for the honesty of his request.

a: If I suffer, it will be because you wished it
p: Ignatius turns the usual meaning upside down: to let him die is kindness, to save him is hate.
b: Greek ean pathō, ēthelēsate; ean apodokimasthō, emisēsate, 'if I suffer, you willed; if I am rejected, you hated'. Lake: 'If I suffer, it was your favour: if I be rejected, it was your hatred.' 'Rejected' is the word for a candidate or a coin that fails the test: if he is turned back from martyrdom, he has been found unfit.
orig: ἐὰν πάθω, ἠθελήσατε· ἐὰν ἀποδοκιμασθῶ, ἐμισήσατε

a: Jesus Christ alone will oversee it
p: The verb is the verb of 'overseer': with its bishop gone, Christ will be Antioch's overseer.
b: Greek monos autēn Iēsous Christos episkopēsei, from episkopeō, the verb behind episkopos, 'overseer'. Lake: 'Its bishop shall be Jesus Christ alone,—and your love.' God is its shepherd 'in my place', and 1 Peter calls Christ 'the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls' (1 Peter 2:25). Ignatius, who in other letters says nothing should be done without the overseer, here leaves his own church to Christ and to the prayers of a church far away. Lake's introduction names, as one of Ignatius's motives, his anxiety 'to secure the future of his own church in Antioch'.

a: one born at the wrong time
p: Ignatius takes Paul's word for himself in 1 Corinthians 15:8.
b: Greek ektrōma, a child born dead or too early, a miscarriage. Lake's margin gives 1 Corinthians 15:8-9: 'Last of all, as to one born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also' (1 Corinthians 15:8), followed by 'For I am the least of the apostles'. Ignatius borrows both: 'the last of them' and 'one born at the wrong time'. The digital text prints hōn ('of whom'); the sense needs the participle ōn, 'being', and the Plain English Translation reads it so ('since I am the last of them').

a: went ahead of me from city to city
p: Churches sent people ahead to meet him at each stop, even cities off his route.
b: Greek kata polin me proēgon, 'city by city they went before me'. Lightfoot and Lake take it of delegates sent ahead to meet him. His other letters name such visitors: from Ephesus, Magnesia and Tralles at Smyrna. 'Not as a passerby': they treated him as one who belonged to them. Polycarp later thanks the Philippians for escorting prisoners 'wrapped in chains fit for saints' (Polycarp to the Philippians 1:1).
r: Polycarp to the Philippians 1:1; Acts 28:15; 3 John 1:6

a: From Smyrna
p: Eusebius says Ignatius wrote four letters at Smyrna, this one among them.
b: Eusebius: when he was at Smyrna, 'where Polycarp was', he wrote one letter to the church at Ephesus, another to the one at Magnesia on the Maeander, and another to the one at Tralles, and 'besides these he writes also to the church of the Romans' (Church History 3.36.5-6). 'By the Ephesians' (di' Ephesiōn) means the Ephesian delegates are carrying the letter or helping him send it. Smyrna is one of the seven churches of Revelation (Revelation 2:8-11).

a: Crocus
p: A friend with Ignatius at Smyrna, named also in the letter to the Ephesians.
b: Greek Krokos, to pothēton moi onoma, 'Crocus, the name longed for by me': a way of saying 'my dear Crocus'. In his letter to the Ephesians Ignatius names a Crocus, 'worthy of God and of you', who 'refreshed' him (Ignatius to the Ephesians 2:1).

a: those who went ahead of me from Syria to Rome
p: Some Christians from Syria had gone on to Rome before him.
b: Ignatius does not name them or say why they went. He asks the Romans to tell them he is near and to 'refresh' them, the verb Paul uses of those who cheered his spirit (1 Corinthians 16:18; Philemon 1:7).

a: the ninth day before the Kalends of September
p: A Roman date: Lake renders it 24 August. The year is not given.
b: The Romans counted days back from the Kalends, the first of each month, counting both ends. Lake renders the date 'the 24th of August'. The Roberts and Donaldson translation has 'on the day before the ninth of the Kalends of September (that is, on the twenty-third day of August)': it is translating a differently worded date, 'the day before the ninth', not the same words read another way. No year is given. Eusebius's Chronicle, as Lake reports, puts the martyrdom 'in the tenth year of Trajan, i.e. 108 A.D.'; Jerome says he suffered in 'the eleventh year of Trajan' (anno undecimo Trajani, Lives of Illustrious Men 16).

a: in the endurance of Jesus Christ
p: Lake's margin gives 2 Thessalonians 3:5.
b: Greek en hypomonē Iēsou Christou. Paul prays: 'May the Lord lead your hearts straight into the love of God and into the endurance of Christ' (2 Thessalonians 3:5). Hypomonē is endurance under suffering, the word of Revelation 1:9.
